newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - New Japan forex law frees credit policy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New Japan forex law frees credit policy.

text.p: Sweeping changes in Japan's foreign exchange law would free the massive capital confined here and could loosen the grip that Tokyo's powerful monetary authorities have over credit policies, analysts say.

The revisions, to be implemented next April, will also allow Japan's financial authorities to track the flow of global capital by enforcing that all large cross-border transactions in the market be reported.

In its first drastic reform of the Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law in 17 years, Japan will scrap dozens of regulations and allow its companies and individuals to deal directly with overseas banks and brokers.
As the yen becomes held more globally, analysts say that Japanese monetary authorities may lose some of their broad control over the country's interest rates.

"More substantial and rapid cross-border capital flows will mean that the scope for policy manoeuvres by Japanese monetary authorities will be reduced," said Takashi Hosomi, chairman of the NLI Research Institute, a research arm of Japan's largest insurer Nippon Life Insurance.

The Bank of Japan (BOJ) can no longer put in place arbitrary credit policies -- possible when the circulation of yen was confined within Japan -- and not expect global markets to react, said Hosomi, a former vice finance minister for international affairs.

"In other words, the expansive role played by Japanese monetary policy in domestic markets would be lessened to some extent," Hosomi said, adding that domestic interest rate policy will settle back to its original purpose.
Such arbitrary credit policies by Japan have resulted in financial chaos in the past.
Monetary authorities have admitted that a delay in tightening monetary policy in 1987-89 was critical in creating Japan's asset inflation "bubble" in those years.
Then, the BOJ had held down rates for the sake of international policy coordination, while ignoring the exuberance of Japan's asset prices.

BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita has played down fears that the central bank would lose its control, however, arguing that most Japanese companies are unlikely to move settlement procedures offshore, given the cost.
Therefore, he said, the legislative change is unlikely to reduce the effectiveness of the BOJ's monetary policy.
AUTHORITIES WATCHFUL OF CAPITAL FLOWS
The new forex law will also force monetary authorities to monitor capital flows much more closely.
"The new forex law would further increase the velocity of money," Kosuke Nakahira, a special advisor to Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, told Reuters.
"This suggests that the monetary authorities will have to pay closer attention to the global capital flows when deciding the timing for monetary policy changes," he added.
But the determining factor for monetary policy will always be economic fundamentals, not capital flows, he added.

Under the revision, the trail of money will be programmed to appear on the Ministry of Finance's (MOF) radar screen as banks, brokers and corporations will have to report large cross-border transactions that could affect exchange rates.

"The limit on how big the deals need to be to be reported should be set individually according to the purpose of the transactions, such as direct and securities investment," an MOF official told Reuters.
The MOF is also keen to spot capital flows generated by speculators who are quick to detect any changes in the trend.
"We will demand that global currency speculators who operate in Tokyo also report their deals," the official said.
STRICTER PUNISHMENT FOR LAPSES
A failure or a lapse in reporting the details of the transaction will subject the person responsible to a sentence of up to six months, the official said.
Punishment also exists under the current law, which allows only licenced banks to make currency deals, but none have been punished so far.
The new forex legislation will abolish the licenced forex banks system and allow everybody to tap the currency market.
"Under the new rules, the punishment for breaking the rule should naturally be stricter," the MOF official said.
A shift in credit policy in a major economy -- or even the expectation of it -- can throw world financial markets into a frenzy as players switch capital from one market to another.
In May, market expectations that Japan may nudge up its rock-bottom interest rates not only drove up the yen and yen bond yields, but upset the U.S. Treasury market.
Expectation of rising yen interest rates forced hedge fund managers to dump billions of dollars of U.S. Treasury bonds in the market.

Those highly-leveraged investment funds had been active in the so-called "yen carry trade" in which they borrow low-cost yen funds and convert them into dollars through swap markets for U.S. Treasuries and equities investment.
But the subsequent rises in yen interest rates in response to a fears of tighter credit have forced the funds to pay back yen by cashing in the U.S. Treasuries.
In Asia, Japanese monetary policy has been blamed as the main catalyst for the recent, speculative attacks on various Asian currencies, most notably the Thai baht.
Many southeast Asian countries are heavily indebted to Japan, a consequence of its cheap yen and low lending rates.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in a recent research report that in the case of Thailand, two-thirds of its outstanding debt is owed to Japanese banks, suggesting that any increase in Japanese rates will lead to a higher cost of capital for the economically troubled country.
MONETARY POLICIES MAY SYNCHRONISE IN MAJOR NATIONS
Analysts noted that the change in Japan's forex law is likely to make interest rates of major economies move in a similar direction at a similar timing.

"When capital flow volumes increase, opportunities for interest rate arbitrage would naturally rise, making interest rates of major economies move in a more concerted manner and influence each other," said Kagehide Kaku, deputy chairman of Daiwa Institute of Research.
But such synchronisation would be offset in part by foreign exchange market moves, added Kaku, the former director of the Bank of Japan's Bank Supervision Department.
MOF's Nakahira said: "(A synchronised monetary policy) would be possible only under a fixed exchange rate mechanism."
Committing to a fixed currency system would mean major economies will need to adopt similar policies even at the cost of domestic economic growth, he said.

"But if we continue to support the current exchange rate mechanism in which currency rates can fluctuate freely, reflecting the underlying economy, economic policies should be different in each country," Nakahira said.
